Notion of continuity Intuitively , a function is continuous at a point if the graph can be drawn through the point without lifting your pencil (there are no holes or jumps in the graph at that point). Definition. A function y = f ( x ) is continuous at a if f ( a ) is defined and lim f ( x ) = f ( a ) . x → a

Continuity checklist We will use the following checklist to determine if a given function y = f ( x ) is continuous at a given point x = a : ( i ) Is f ( a ) defined? ( ii ) Does lim x → a f ( x ) exist? ( iii ) Does lim x → a f ( x ) = f ( a ) ? If the answer to each of these is YES, then f is continuous at x = a . If the answer to any of these is NO, then f is not continuous at x = a .

Intermediate Value Theorem The Intermediate Value Theorem says that if a continuous function has two different y -values, then it takes on every y -value between those two values. The precise statement of the theorem is the following. Theorem. If y = f ( x ) is continuous on the interval [ a , b ] and m is any number in ( f ( a ) , f ( b )) , then there is a number c , with a < c < b , such that f ( c ) = m .

Intermediate Value Theorem (geometric interpretation) Alternatively, suppose we have two points in the xy -plane and we draw a horizontal line between them at y = m . In order to draw the graph of a continuous function y = f ( x ) between the points, we must cross the line y = m somewhere. The x -coordinate of the intersection point is the number c in the theorem.
